evidence_level: associated (three independent programs and evaluators; adjustment for prior achievement to be confirmed in at least two)
pathway: Taking part in an after-school program regularly over several years (three or more years in elementary school, or three or more semesters in high school) is associated with lower dropout and higher on-time graduation than similar non-participants.
model_match: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
typical_effect: LA's BEST: high-participation students about 5 percent less likely to drop out and 6 percent more likely to graduate on time (low attenders no benefit); After School Matters: three or more semesters went with higher graduation and lower dropout after controlling prior attendance; Citizen Schools: former participants graduated at higher rates than matched peers. All leads until checked.
caveats: Dose-selection: the comparisons set long-term attenders against non-attenders, so the gap may reflect who stays. The one randomized trial of a high school after-school program with school-record outcomes (After School Matters, Q-P03) found no school-performance effect, and the national 21st CCLC trial (L-12) found no academic effects. Associated tier only if at least two of Q-001 to Q-004 adjust for prior achievement or prior attendance; otherwise D and not recommended. Never use the federal GPRA 'share improved' measure as support.
rationale: This is the 21st CCLC-adjacent long-term evidence the first review lacked. Three independent programs (LA's BEST, CRESST; After School Matters, Chapin Hall; Citizen Schools, Policy Studies Associates) point the same way on S3/S4 with district records. None is a trial, so it fits the associated tier at best, and its practical message is dosage and retention over years (A2.5), which is a low-cost lever. Q-005 checks whether California's statewide 21st CCLC/ASES evaluation adds a graduation estimate. S-0061 (King & Garcia 2016) supports the dosage pattern on an early-warning index only and is not used as evidence for S3/S4.

evidence_level: C (suggestive; one Philadelphia school, one cohort, matched comparison)
pathway: After-school programming combined with case management for off-track ninth graders raised four-year graduation at one Philadelphia high school, but did not change school-leaving.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: Congreso's Exito, after-school programming plus case management for students with early-warning flags, at Kensington Creative and Performing Arts High School.
typical_effect: Graduation 15 percentage points higher than matched non-participants; no significant effect on school-leaving.
caveats: Single school, single cohort, propensity matching on observables; dropout (S3) null. The strongest Philadelphia partner evidence on S4 found, and a good model for a partner-run replication with a data-sharing agreement.
rationale: Below the bar for tested (single small quasi-experiment gives suggestive at most) but Philadelphia-specific and directly partner-run; listing it keeps the claim bounded: graduation suggestive, dropout null. S-0586 is the 2011 program description, not an impact study.

pathway: A paid after-school apprenticeship program for Chicago high school students did not improve job skills or school performance in a randomized trial.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: No difference in marketable job skills; school-record outcomes null (to confirm).
caveats: Use as bounding evidence for Q-P01: the correlational After School Matters graduation gap did not appear as a school effect in the trial.
rationale: A randomized null on the same program whose correlational study supports Q-P01; the brief's rule that a trial outweighs correlational gaps applies.

evidence_level: none for S4 (graduation predicted, not observed)
pathway: A multi-year comprehensive out-of-school program raised ninth-grade credits and grades for low-achieving lottery winners, but graduation was predicted, not measured.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: StudentU (Durham, NC), summer plus after-school academic, nutrition and social support from middle school into high school.
typical_effect: Low-baseline lottery winners: +0.82 credits and +0.37 GPA points in ninth grade; predicted graduation +4 percentage points.
caveats: Same rule as L-04 and L-30: on-track gains cannot stand in for a graduation effect. Revisit when the graduation follow-up is published.
rationale: S-0040 and S-0380 are the journal and working-paper versions of one lottery study. Strong design, but the indicator itself is not observed.

evidence_level: C (two independent matched quasi-experiments, Chicago and Boston; no randomized trial)
pathway: An after-school competitive policy debate team, with weekly practice and interscholastic tournaments, raised high school graduation compared with similar students in two cities.
model_match: An after-school competitive policy debate team in an urban debate league (regular practice plus interscholastic tournaments) for middle or high school students; the partner shows its own students' graduation from school records against a comparison group.
typical_effect: Debaters more likely to graduate than matched peers (Chicago); evidence of positive graduation effects (Boston); sizes to be filled from Q-009 and Q-010.
caveats: Self-selection into debate is addressed only on observables. Promote only if the checker confirms that both studies control prior achievement for the graduation estimate and that Boston's graduation estimate is significant; otherwise not-recommended at C. The Chicago journal articles (S-0044, S-0301) use the same data and count as one study.
rationale: Two independent cities and research teams, both using district records and matching or fixed effects, both positive on graduation, with Boston also positive on the state ELA test. This meets 'replicated' better than most partner models found. It is a model partners can run.

pathway: The monitoring and mentoring program showed no effect on graduation for general-education students at risk, in a three-year randomized trial.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: No statistically significant impact on graduation (553 students, San Diego).
caveats: Adds a modern randomized null in the general-education population most partners serve.
rationale: Confirms L-24's not-recommended status with a larger, more recent trial in the population partners serve.

pathway: The positive dropout result for monitoring and mentoring comes from students with disabilities; a later trial with general-education students found no effect on dropping out.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: No statistically significant impact on the likelihood of dropping out.
caveats: Add to caveats: the 1998 and 2005 positive trials (S-0098, S-0102) were with students with learning, emotional or behavioral disabilities; the 2018 general-education trial was null. Partners should not claim dropout reduction from Check and Connect-style mentoring for general-education students.
rationale: A null in the general population outweighs the two small positive trials for the claim partners would make.

evidence_level: C (meta-analyses with no single model; effects shrink with study quality)
pathway: Dropout prevention programs as a group raise school completion slightly, but the effect shrinks in higher-quality and unpublished studies, and no single program type stands out.
model_match: Not used for credit: the meta-analyses pool many program types, so they name no model a partner could run. Implementation quality is the strongest moderator.
typical_effect: Average effect about 0.19 standard deviations on completion (2010-2022 studies); positive across program types in 2011 review, with mentoring not significant.
caveats: Outcomes mix self-report, program-defined completion and records; most studies are small. Use for guidance (implementation quality, monitoring attendance) rather than for credit.
rationale: These are the main dropout meta-analyses, previously cited only through Check and Connect. Their own moderator finding (higher-quality methods give smaller effects) and the large-scale nulls in Q-P09 to Q-P12 argue against a tested link. S-0612 is the journal summary of the S-0321 Campbell review (one study); S-0317 (CrimeSolutions practice profile) and S-0505 (evidence gap map) are secondary and need no claim.

evidence_level: B (multi-site randomized null outweighs positive pilot)
pathway: A four-year, year-round program of mentoring, tutoring, service and stipends did not raise high school graduation in its multi-site randomized demonstration, despite a positive pilot.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit. Model checked: the Quantum Opportunity Program (and the later Eisenhower Quantum Opportunities version).
typical_effect: Multi-site demonstration: no significant effect on diploma receipt; 1990s pilot and a later Eisenhower trial reported higher graduation.
caveats: Philadelphia was a pilot site. Under the brief's rule a null at scale outweighs a positive pilot; the Eisenhower trial (Q-018) is a single newer trial and does not reverse that. Merge note: S-0071 carries a Torgesen et al. (2006) reading-trial citation over QOP findings and should be split.
rationale: Intensive multi-year youth development with incentives is exactly what many partners describe; the at-scale null tells them not to claim graduation from it.

pathway: Federally funded middle school dropout prevention programs (mentoring, peer support groups, counseling) did not reduce dropping out in randomized trials.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: No significant difference in dropout or highest grade completed.
caveats: 1990s programs; still the largest randomized test of targeted middle school dropout prevention.
rationale: S-0107 merges nine WWC rows from the same Mathematica report covering several programs (for example Twelve Together); one study for screening purposes.

pathway: Student advocates assigned to at-risk ninth graders in Baltimore did not improve attendance, promotion or graduation in a randomized trial.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: Nonsignificant effects on graduation and related outcomes.
caveats: S-0616 and S-0825 are the same article.
rationale: A direct randomized null for the advocate or case-manager model partners often run in high schools.

pathway: A large randomized trial of a mature comprehensive student-support program in two urban districts found no overall effect on graduation; a school-level matched study of Communities In Schools found gains, but the trials outweigh it.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: Graduation effect small and not significant (n = 2,528); school-level matched study reported larger graduation gains and dropout declines in CIS schools.
caveats: Name the program in Q-021 once checked. Record Porowski and Passa (school-level, public-use data, self-selected schools) as weaker evidence that does not change the tier.
rationale: Adds the largest graduation trial found and documents why the CIS quasi-experiment does not overturn the MDRC trial. S-0416 and S-0617 are the same article.

evidence_level: C (one-school trial, subgroup effect; later trial null on intermediates)
pathway: Twelfth-grade peer leaders running weekly groups for incoming ninth graders raised four-year graduation for boys at one school, but the full-sample effect was not significant and a later multi-school trial found no effect on credits, promotion or attendance.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit. Model checked: Peer Group Connection (Center for Supportive Schools).
typical_effect: Boys: 81 percent against 63 percent graduated; later trial: no significant effects.
caveats: Subgroup finding from one school; replication null on on-track steps.
rationale: A near-peer, low-cost model partners like; the evidence supports neither a graduation claim nor an attendance claim. S-0611 is a dissertation on the same school and adds no independent design.

evidence_level: none for S4 (on-track only; school-run model)
pathway: A whole-ninth-grade relationships model with teacher teams and weekly lessons raised core-course passing and credits in several randomized trials, including at scale, but graduation was not measured.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: BARR (Building Assets, Reducing Risks), run by the school's ninth-grade teachers.
typical_effect: Passing all core courses and credits up (g about 0.2 to 0.3); chronic absence down in the scale-up; persistence to 10th grade not significant.
caveats: Same rule as L-04: on-track gains do not stand in for graduation. School-run, not partner-run. Flag the chronic-absence result to the attendance (S1) screener.
rationale: The best-replicated ninth-grade on-track evidence in the candidate set; recording it prevents partners claiming S4 from relationship-building alone while showing what moves the on-track step.

evidence_level: none for S3/S4 (one-year on-track outcomes; null on completion in Norway)
pathway: A school early-warning and monitoring system cut chronic absence and course failure after one year in a randomized trial, but a Norwegian trial found no effect on completion.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: the Early Warning Intervention and Monitoring System run by school teams.
typical_effect: Lower chronic absence and course failure after one year (US); no significant effect on absence or completion (Norway).
caveats: School-run; outcomes are on-track steps. Partners who use school data to target students can cite it as a practice, not as an S3/S4 effect.
rationale: Bounds L-81's tracking condition: monitoring helps the on-track step but has not shown a completion effect.

pathway: Regular one-to-one school-based mentoring with behavioral monitoring raised credits and cut suspensions for at-risk tenth and eleventh graders in a randomized trial; graduation not measured.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: Achievement Mentoring (weekly mentor meetings with monitoring of grades, attendance and behavior).
typical_effect: Positive on credits and suspensions (sizes to confirm).
caveats: On-track step only; flag attendance result to the S1 screener. Earlier Achievement Mentoring trial (S-0303) was mixed.
rationale: Recorded so a partner running this model knows the S4 claim is not supported yet.

evidence_level: B (mixed: 1990s multi-site trial null on completion; one contemporary lottery positive)
pathway: Career academies did not raise high school completion overall in the 1990s multi-site trial, but a contemporary technology academy raised graduation by about 8 points in a lottery study.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: a school-within-a-school career academy; schools, not partners, run it.
typical_effect: Contemporary lottery: graduation +8 percentage points, mainly boys; ninth-grade absences down. 1990s trial: no overall effect on completion.
caveats: Keep not-recommended for partners (school model). Revise the pathway and caveats to show the newer lottery result, and note that it is one academy in one district.
rationale: L-77 currently reads as uniformly null; the Wake County lottery is new randomized evidence that changes the wording though not the tier. S-0718 (JROTC career academies, matched) and S-0487 (difference in differences) are weaker and need no claim.

evidence_level: B for the school model, not a partner link
pathway: Admission to a CTE high school in Philadelphia went with higher graduation and credit accumulation; in Baltimore, admission raised CTE pathway completion but lowered GPA.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: full-time attendance at a CTE high school.
typical_effect: Philadelphia: better graduation and credit accumulation (size to confirm); Baltimore: pathway completion up, GPA down.
caveats: Adds Philadelphia-specific evidence. Keep not-recommended for partners. NYC CTE high school lottery report (S-0838) is a lead without results in hand.
rationale: Philadelphia evidence for the existing CTE link. S-0482 and S-0837 are the same Baltimore study.

evidence_level: associated (if two of Q-033 to Q-035 confirm controls for prior achievement)
pathway: Taking CTE courses and earning industry certifications in high school is associated with higher on-time graduation, including in Philadelphia, after accounting for prior achievement and behavior.
model_match: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
typical_effect: Philadelphia: CTE participation associated with higher four-year graduation, including for students entering tenth grade with strong risk flags; Florida: earning certifications raised on-time graduation, more for at-risk students.
caveats: Coursework and certifications are school-delivered; partners who run certification preparation or pre-apprenticeships can cite the association only. Selection into CTE remains.
rationale: Fills the gap between L-79 (certification as the S13 measure) and S4. S-0479 and S-0839 are one study. S-0840 and S-0512 are leads without results.

evidence_level: C (one Philadelphia cohort, matched on rich pre-program data)
pathway: School-to-career and college-encouragement programs in Philadelphia high schools in the 1990s went with higher graduation and less dropout than matched students.
model_match: Not used for credit. Model checked: high school school-to-career and college-encouragement programs in Philadelphia.
typical_effect: Positive effects on graduation and similar negative effects on dropout (sizes to confirm).
caveats: One cohort, programs not described as a single model, 1990s.
rationale: Philadelphia-specific; recorded so the map shows it was checked.

evidence_level: B for the school model, not a partner link
pathway: Attending an early college high school raised high school graduation in lottery-based randomized studies in several states and in North Carolina.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: a stand-alone early college high school; school systems, not partners, run it.
typical_effect: Graduation higher for lottery winners (multi-state and North Carolina; sizes to confirm).
caveats: Contrast with L-78 (P-TECH career early college: no four-year graduation effect). Keep as context like L-74 and L-96.
rationale: Replicated randomized positives that should be in the map as context; they bound L-78. S-0846 (early college strategies in comprehensive schools) and S-0848 (dual enrollment meta-analysis, college outcomes) need no claim.

pathway: Career-focused learning, paid internships and work-based learning programs for high school students did not raise high school enrollment or completion in randomized trials.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit. Models checked: Youth CareerConnect, Urban Alliance internships.
typical_effect: Youth CareerConnect: no effect on being enrolled in high school; Urban Alliance: graduation effect to confirm.
caveats: Urban Alliance served seniors, most of whom graduate anyway. 12 for Life (S-0489, matched, null on GPA) is a lead only.
rationale: Career exploration statements are common in partner logic models; the trials say not to claim S3/S4 from them.

pathway: A federal college-access program (Talent Search) did not change high school completion in a matched evaluation.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: No significant effect on earning a diploma or GED (WWC review).
caveats: Pairs with L-80 (Upward Bound).
rationale: Second federal college-access program checked against S4; same answer as L-80.

pathway: Students who took an AVID elective graduated at higher rates than matched peers, but schoolwide AVID in rural Florida made little difference to graduation.
model_match: Not used for credit. Model checked: AVID (school-run elective or schoolwide).
typical_effect: Matched study: higher graduation for elective completers; schoolwide study: little difference in graduation or credits.
caveats: Elective completers are selected on persistence; the schoolwide estimate is closer to a policy effect.
rationale: Mixed evidence; recorded so partners supporting AVID do not claim S4.

pathway: A meta-analysis of GEAR UP evaluations reports higher graduation for participants, but most included evaluations may lack strong comparison groups.
model_match: Not used for credit. Model checked: GEAR UP cohort college-readiness grants.
typical_effect: Graduation rate higher for participants (pooled size to confirm).
caveats: Promote only if Q-044 shows the graduation estimate rests on matched or randomized studies.
rationale: S-0849 and S-0498 are one meta-analysis. Kept below the bar pending the design check.

evidence_level: B (the evidence is real, but it measures a different outcome)
pathway: Programs for young people who have already left school (YouthBuild, National Guard Youth ChalleNGe, JOBSTART) raise diploma or GED receipt in some trials, but this is not the District's four-year graduation rate or its dropout count.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: YouthBuild: diploma or equivalency up; ChalleNGe and JOBSTART: diploma or GED effects to confirm (WWC rows show not significant).
caveats: Re-engagement partners can claim Y1.17 re-engagement and credentials, never S3 or S4.
rationale: Prevents a common category error in logic models. New Chance (S-0066), Job Corps (S-0313) and service corps (S-0070, S-0760) are in the same position and need no separate claim.

pathway: Cash rewards to families or teen parents for school attendance and progress did not reliably raise graduation or lower dropout in randomized trials.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit. Models checked: Opportunity NYC Family Rewards and Family Rewards 2.0, Ohio LEAP, the California School Attendance Demonstration.
typical_effect: Family Rewards: some high school gains for students proficient at entry, no graduation change to confirm; Family Rewards 2.0: no effect on school progress; LEAP and the attendance demonstration: no effect on completion or dropout.
caveats: LEAP raised short-term enrollment and attendance (S-0830), which is an S1 question.
rationale: Recorded nulls for an F2.1 pathway partners sometimes claim (stipends, incentives).

pathway: Winning a summer jobs lottery in Boston raised on-time graduation and cut dropout; trials of summer jobs in Chicago and in the 1980s STEP program found no schooling gains.
model_match: Unchanged: a paid summer job placement for low-income high school students, ideally allocated or evaluated by lottery.
typical_effect: Unchanged for Boston; add: Chicago One Summer Plus (two cohorts) no average schooling effect; STEP no long-term dropout effect.
caveats: Cite the nulls by name in the caveats. Methods reviewer to decide whether Chicago's null on school persistence is a failed replication that should demote this row; screener's view is revise, because Chicago targeted violence prevention with mostly older youth and measured persistence, not the graduation indicator.
rationale: Makes the 'nulls elsewhere' caveat checkable. S-0835 (NYC, college outcomes) and S-0491 (popular summary of the Boston study already in L-72) need no claim.

pathway: A first-grade classroom behavior-management game raised the odds of high school graduation in a Baltimore randomized trial.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: the Good Behavior Game as part of a classroom-centered first-grade program, run by teachers.
typical_effect: Greater odds of high school graduation at age 19 (size to confirm).
caveats: One trial and cohort; teacher-run; effects may differ by gender. A low-cost practice partners could adapt to group settings, but untested there.
rationale: Relevant to the low-cost-strategy question but not enough for a tested link.

pathway: Social-skills groups for disruptive kindergarten boys plus parent training raised later school completion in a Montreal randomized trial.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: the Montreal Prevention Program.
typical_effect: Higher completion or lower dropout at follow-up (size to confirm).
caveats: Single small trial, non-US, boys only.
rationale: Same study in two rows. Recorded as checked and below the bar.

evidence_level: C (one trial; outcome source to confirm)
pathway: A family program for Mexican American families at the move to middle school reduced later dropping out in a randomized trial.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: Bridges to High School (Puentes): parent, adolescent and family group sessions in seventh grade.
typical_effect: Fewer students dropped out (WWC g about 0.54).
caveats: One trial in one region; if dropout is self-reported it does not meet the District-count bar.
rationale: A partner-runnable family model with a direct dropout outcome; suggestive only.

pathway: Elective classes for Black male students taught by Black male teachers, with a focus on identity, history and academic support, reduced Black male dropout in Oakland.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: Oakland's African American Male Achievement (Manhood Development) classes, district-run.
typical_effect: Significant reduction in Black male dropout, smaller reduction for Black females, mainly in ninth grade.
caveats: One district; school-run elective; staggered rollout not random.
rationale: The only Y5.2 evidence on S3 found; suggestive. S-0494 and S-0858 are one study.

pathway: Social and emotional learning gains persist years later, but two randomized trials of early SEL programs that followed students to the end of high school found no direct effect on on-time graduation.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: INSIGHTS (NYC, 13-year follow-up): graduation effect to confirm, early gains faded by middle school; Head Start REDI: no direct impact on on-time graduation.
caveats: Replace 'graduation was rarely measured' with the two trials' results.
rationale: New graduation evidence that changes L-14's wording but keeps its tier.

pathway: School-based health centers did not reduce dropout in a newer quasi-experiment and were not associated with graduation in a matched school-level study.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: No effect on dropout rates; suspensions per suspended student down 10 to 26 percent.
rationale: Confirms L-65 with two further studies.

pathway: Community schools in Tennessee did not change dropout rates, though they raised English language arts scores slightly.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: No change in dropout rate; small ELA gains; chronic absence rose.
caveats: Bounds L-37 and L-40. Pass the chronic-absence increase to the S1 screener (it bears on L-36).
rationale: A direct S3 null for community schools.

pathway: The What Works Clearinghouse found no Teen Outreach Program study that met its standards.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: Not applicable.
caveats: Supports the drop already applied to L-97.
rationale: Independent confirmation that the TOP evidence is thin.

pathway: Online credit recovery did not do better than teacher-led credit recovery in randomized trials; in Chicago, fewer students recovered credit online.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: Chicago: online students less likely to recover algebra credit, no long-term difference; LAUSD: effects on credits and graduation to confirm.
caveats: Relevant to partners that host credit recovery.
rationale: S-0599 (newcomer English learners, triple differences) is a lead without results.

pathway: Chronic absence in the upper elementary and middle grades is associated with lower high school completion, in the Chicago Longitudinal Study and in a district attendance-trajectory study.
model_match: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
typical_effect: Sizes to confirm.
caveats: Count toward L-101 only if the controls include earlier achievement.
rationale: Two more independent longitudinal studies for L-101.

pathway: A meta-analysis of predictors of on-time graduation confirms that course performance predicts graduating in four years.
model_match: Unchanged.
typical_effect: Pooled predictor sizes to confirm.
caveats: Use only if Q-067 shows grades, course failure or credits among significant predictors.
rationale: Meta-analytic support for the existing predictor row.

evidence_level: associated (meta-analysis of associations; adjustment to be confirmed)
pathway: Supportive family processes, such as parental involvement, support and monitoring, are associated with lower dropout.
model_match: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
typical_effect: Pooled association to confirm; in NELS:88 involvement explained dropout and truancy but not achievement.
caveats: Associations of this kind are often unadjusted for prior achievement; keep at associated only if Q-068 confirms a pooled association with dropout. May duplicate a family-engagement screener's proposal.
rationale: S-0430 and S-0623 are one meta-analysis. L-34 covers achievement only, not dropout.

evidence_level: C (one site, non-US difference in differences)
pathway: A community-agency program combining tutoring, mentoring, family support and financial incentives raised high school graduation in a Toronto public-housing neighborhood.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: Pathways to Education, run by community agencies.
typical_effect: Graduation up sharply at the first site (size to confirm).
caveats: One site, Canada; expansion sites may show smaller effects (check Q-070 and any follow-up). Close cousin of the Quantum Opportunity Program, which was null at scale in the US (Q-P09).
rationale: Highly partner-like model with a large effect; suggestive only. S-0281 (New Brunswick Learning Accounts, incentive accounts) is a separate Canadian lead without a claim.

evidence_level: C (small 1990s trial; staying enrolled, not the District count)
pathway: Attendance monitoring, counseling and family outreach for middle school Latino students kept more students enrolled through ninth grade, but not significantly through eleventh grade.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: ALAS (Achievement for Latinos through Academic Success).
typical_effect: Enrolled at end of 9th grade: significant; end of 11th grade: not significant.
caveats: Small sample; staying enrolled is not the District dropout count; effect faded.
rationale: Same position as L-23.

pathway: A community mentoring program for off-track middle and high school students did not improve attendance, behavior or course passing over three years compared with matched students.
model_match: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
typical_effect: No significant effects.
caveats: Matched comparison in five districts.
rationale: Another mentoring null on the on-track step.
